event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: RJF’s 2022 filing couches pandemic matters largely in the context of macro-level uncertainty but still concedes a concrete, on-going operational hit: an unusually tight post-COVID labour market that is affecting every part of the business.  Most language is forward-looking and qualified ("may be impacted"), signalling potential rather than booked losses, yet the firm explicitly notes that it "has been impacted" by pandemic-related labour turnover.  The discussion therefore mixes generic boiler-plate with at least one clear admission of present-day impact.  Because the filing date (Nov-2022) is within three years of the WHO declaration (Mar-2020), the Time Decay Principle allows higher scores, but the absence of quantified dollar figures tempers severity.  Overall, the evidence points to a moderate-to-high continuing risk (labour shortages, market volatility) rather than an existential or heavily quantified threat.

evidence_list.snippet: The labor market continues to experience elevated levels of turnover in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and we have been impacted by an extremely competitive labor market, including increased competition for talent across all aspects of our business, as well as increased competition with non-traditional competitors, such as technology companies.

components.reason: Directly links current labour-force problems to the COVID-19 pandemic (‘in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic’).
States an existing, realised effect on the company (‘we have been impacted’).
Describes an ongoing condition (‘continues to experience’) indicating persistence of risk.
Highlights broad operational scope (talent across all aspects, competition with tech firms) which enlarges potential impact.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: This sentence earns a high score (8/10) because it admits a concrete, continuing post-COVID impact on the firm’s operations and talent costs, without offering any mitigating action or limitation.

evidence_list.snippet: U.S. markets may also be impacted by public health epidemics or pandemics, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as by political and civil unrest occurring in other parts of the world.

components.reason: Explicitly references the COVID-19 pandemic as an example of a risk driver.
Connects pandemics to broader market impacts, implying indirect risk to the firm through market channels.
Use of conditional and generic phrasing (‘may’) dilutes immediacy.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: The sentence recognises COVID-19 as a potential market shock but is couched in broad, conditional terms; thus it receives a moderate score of 3/10.

evidence_list.snippet: Macroeconomic conditions may also be negatively impacted by domestic or international events, including natural disasters, political unrest, or public health epidemics and pandemics, as well as by a number of factors in the global financial markets that may be detrimental to our operating results.

components.reason: Lists ‘public health epidemics and pandemics’ as a factor that can harm operating results.
Specifies that such impacts could be ‘detrimental to our operating results’, linking event to firm performance.
Highly generic; pandemics are one item in a long list, and risk is framed as possible (‘may’).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: This is largely boiler-plate, acknowledging pandemics only as one of many vague macro risks, so it scores a low-moderate 2/10.
